questions.q: Define irony and symbolism in your own words, giving one example from everyday life for each.
questions.a: Irony: a situation where the outcome is contrary to what was expected (e.g., a fire station burning down). Symbolism: an object representing a deeper idea (e.g., a dove representing peace). A wrong answer that defines irony as "funny coincidence" reveals confusion between irony and mere chance; a wrong answer that calls any mentioned object a symbol shows inability to distinguish literal from representational meaning.

questions.q: In "Olar Vak", the speaker describes the old man's daily routine: "The sun rises, the birds sing, the old man waits." Explain the situational irony in this depiction of waiting.
questions.a: The irony lies in the contrast between the vibrant, cyclical renewal of nature (sun, birds) and the old man's static, linear wait for an end that does not come. Nature's "morning" symbolizes beginnings, while the old man's wait is for a final ending — the two temporal orders clash. A wrong answer that only lists the routine without naming the contrast misses the analytical core; a student who calls it "sadness" confuses tone with irony.

questions.q: Identify one symbol in "Raksaks" and explain how its meaning shifts across the three stanzas.
questions.a: The "house" (ghar) is the central symbol. In stanza 1 it represents physical shelter ("walls, roof, doors"); in stanza 2 it becomes a metaphor for emotional security ("heart's walls, memory's roof"); in stanza 3 it ironically turns into a pyre ("when the house is ready, we burn it"). A wrong answer that treats the house only as a building fails to track the semantic shift; a student who says "the house symbolizes life" without stanza-by-stanza evidence gives a vague generalization.

questions.q: Compare the use of verbal irony in "Olar Vak" (the old man's speech) with the structural irony in "Raksaks" (the refrain). How does each type serve the poem's theme?
questions.a: In "Olar Vak", verbal irony appears when the old man calls death "my dear friend" (priya mitr) while his body recoils — the gap between word and feeling reveals denial. In "Raksaks", structural irony resides in the refrain "Raksaks, raksaks" which sounds like a construction chant but actually enacts the futility of building against time; the repetition mimics the monotonous, endless labor. A wrong answer that treats both as "irony" without distinguishing verbal vs. structural misses the nuance; a student who says "both show sadness" reduces device to theme.

questions.q: Evaluate which poem uses symbolism more effectively to convey the inevitability of aging. Support your judgment with two textual reasons.
questions.a: "Raksaks" uses symbolism more effectively because (1) the house symbol operates at three semantic levels (physical, emotional, existential) creating a layered architecture of meaning, and (2) the final transformation of house into pyre fuses symbol and irony into a single unforgettable image. "Olar Vak" relies more on imagery than sustained symbols. A wrong answer that picks "Olar Vak" because "it has more symbols" shows quantitative rather than qualitative evaluation; a student who cannot cite specific symbol transformations lacks evidentiary rigor.

questions.q: Write a four-line stanza about an elderly person that uses both verbal irony and a recurring symbol (choose any object). Mark the ironic line and the symbol.
questions.a:
Example:  
"My legs are wings," he laughs, though stairs defeat him — (verbal irony marked)  
The cane he taps writes poems on the floor. (cane = symbol of dignity/voice)  
Each tap a stanza, each pause a rhyme,  
He walks the house he built, now walking him.  
A poor answer uses irony as mere sarcasm ("He's so fast he's slow") or picks a symbol without thematic resonance (e.g., "his watch" without linking to time's passage).
